\chapter{And, Or, But}
\label{ch:gu-and-or-but}
\hlchaptermodality{36}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can join two things or two whole sentences with and, offer a choice with or, set one thing against another with but, and say that something applies too.}

The three coordinators, and the first two-clause sentence this book can make. ane joins two nouns and two whole sentences and costs neither of them anything; athava asks the listener to choose; pan sets one against the other -- and moved to just after a noun, the same word becomes 'also', which is the first time in this book that position alone decides a word's job.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[ane]{\gu{અને} (ane) — and}

\label{lesson:GU-C32-ane}



\begin{quote}
From the chapter behind you, the two sentences that get you out of trouble. Then, from the food chapter far behind you, \textbf{tea} and \textbf{milk}.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{māf karo}, \emph{samajto nathī} — then \emph{chā}, \emph{dūdh}
\end{itemize}

Both of those drinks were taught in the same chapter, on facing pages. Until this lesson there has been no way to ask for both of them in one breath.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\gu{ચા} \gu{અને} \gu{દૂધ}} — \emph{chā ane dūdh} — \textbf{tea and milk}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\gu{અને}} stands between the two things it joins, exactly where English puts \emph{and}. That is the whole of it for now.

It did not start as a joining word. \textbf{\gu{અને}} comes from Sanskrit \textbf{\gu{અન્ય}} (\emph{anya}), \textquotedblleft{}other\textquotedblright{} — so the word that now means \emph{and} began as the word for \textbf{the other one}. Naming a second thing and calling it \textquotedblleft{}the other\textquotedblright{} is how a great many languages built their \emph{and}, and Gujarati still shows the seam.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{chā ane dūdh}.
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{chā} alone, then the pair. Hear what the middle word buys you.
  \item \emph{Build:} pick any two things you can already name, and join them.
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Join two drinks in one phrase. Where does \textbf{\gu{અને}} stand relative to the things it joins? (Between them.) What did it mean before it meant \emph{and}? (\textquotedblleft{}Other\textquotedblright{}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ane (be vākya)]{\gu{અને}, joining two sentences}

\label{lesson:GU-C32-ane-clauses}



\begin{quote}
One lesson back: the joining word, and where it stands. Five lessons back, at the top of the last chapter: the word that replaces \emph{chhe}.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{ane}, and \emph{nathī}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
The same \textbf{\gu{અને}} that joined two nouns joins two whole sentences, and it changes nothing about either one:

\begin{quote}
\emph{(first sentence)} \textbf{\gu{અને}} \emph{(second sentence)}
\end{quote}

Nothing is added to the verbs, nothing moves, and no ending appears. This is why \emph{and} is the joining word to learn first: it is the only one that costs the sentences on either side of it absolutely nothing.

And it composes with what you learned last chapter — the second half is free to be a negative:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{… \gu{અને} … \gu{નથી}} — \textquotedblleft{}… and … is not\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

That is a two-clause sentence, and it is the first one this book has been able to make.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Build:} two short sentences you can already say, joined with \emph{ane}.
  \item \emph{Build:} the same again, with \emph{nathī} closing the second half.
  \item \emph{Contrast:} the two sentences said separately, then joined. Same words.
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What changes about a sentence when \textbf{\gu{અને}} joins it to another? (Nothing at all.) Make one two-clause sentence whose second half is negative.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ane]{\gu{અને} reaches the page}

\label{lesson:GU-C32-ane-write}



\begin{quote}
Say the joining word before anything is uncovered. Then a long reach back — read the word for \textbf{city}, written many chapters ago and not read since.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Read it:} \textbf{\gu{શહેર}}
\end{itemize}

That word has been waiting a long time for a second look; this is it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — three signs, none of them new}
Uncover \textbf{\gu{અને}} once. Name its pieces in order:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\gu{અ}} — the independent \emph{a} · \textbf{\gu{ન}} — \emph{na} · \textbf{\gu{ે}} — the \emph{e} stroke above
\end{quote}

Every one of the three was taught long before this chapter. This is worth saying plainly: the word this book most needed was never a writing problem. It was never written down.

\subsection*{Writing — guided copy, model in view}
Keep the model in view and copy \textbf{\gu{અને}} once. Check the \textbf{\gu{ે}} sits above and to the right of \textbf{\gu{ન}}, not over \textbf{\gu{અ}}.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Write \textbf{\gu{અને}} from memory once, then uncover and compare. How many of its three signs were new today? (None.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[athavā]{\gu{અથવા} (athavā) — or}

\label{lesson:GU-C32-athava}



\begin{quote}
One lesson back you wrote the joining word. Five lessons back, in the middle of the last chapter, you learned to say you had not followed.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} \textbf{\gu{અને}}, and \emph{samajto nathī}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\gu{અને}} offers you both. \textbf{\gu{અથવા}} offers you one of two:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\gu{ચા} \gu{અથવા} \gu{દૂધ}} — \emph{chā athavā dūdh} — \textbf{tea or milk}
\end{quote}

It stands in the same place \emph{ane} does, between the two things, and it asks the listener to pick.

Inside it are two older words: Sanskrit \textbf{\gu{અથ}} (\emph{atha}, \textquotedblleft{}then, moreover\textquotedblright{}) and \textbf{\gu{વા}} (\emph{vā}, \textquotedblleft{}or\textquotedblright{}). Gujarati fused a linking word and a choosing word and kept both.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{chā athavā dūdh} — then \emph{chā ane dūdh}. One asks, one gives.
  \item \emph{Contrast:} the two joining words back to back, twice.
  \item \emph{Build:} offer someone a choice of two things you can name.
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Offer a choice of two drinks, then offer both. Which word did each need? (\emph{athavā} to choose, \emph{ane} to give both.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[paṇ]{\gu{પણ} (paṇ) — but, and also}

\label{lesson:GU-C32-pan}



\begin{quote}
The two joining words so far: one gives both, one asks you to choose. Say them.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{ane}, \emph{athavā}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\gu{પણ}} sets one thing against another. It joins two clauses the way \emph{ane} does, and it warns that the second will pull against the first:

\begin{quote}
\emph{(first sentence)} \textbf{\gu{પણ}} \emph{(second sentence)} — \textquotedblleft{}… \textbf{but} …\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

It works especially well with what you learned last chapter, because the sharpest contrast a beginner can draw is between something that is and something that \textbf{\gu{નથી}}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the same word, moved, means \textquotedblleft{}also\textquotedblright{}}]
Put \textbf{\gu{પણ}} between two clauses and it is \emph{but}. Put it directly \textbf{after a noun} and it becomes \textbf{also}:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\gu{ચા} \gu{પણ}} — \emph{chā paṇ} — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{tea too}\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Nothing about the word changes. Only where it stands changes, and position alone carries the difference. This is the first time in this book that a word's job has depended on its place in the sentence rather than on its ending.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} two clauses joined with \emph{paṇ}, the second one negative.
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{chā paṇ} — the \textquotedblleft{}also\textquotedblright{} reading, straight after a noun.
  \item \emph{Contrast:} \emph{paṇ} between clauses, then \emph{paṇ} after a noun. Same word.
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \emph{tea too}. Now say a sentence that uses \textbf{\gu{પણ}} to mean \emph{but}. What decides which of the two you get? (Where the word stands — after a noun, or between two clauses.) Next chapter: the word that lets you say what somebody \textbf{thinks}.
\end{tcolorbox}
